title: Philomena Schwab: 100,000 wishlists in 3 months - Weird roguelikes are taking over the world
speaker: Philomena Schwab
talk_title: 100,000 wishlists in 3 months - Weird roguelikes are taking over the world
description: The roguelike genre continues to ride a massive wave of popularity. New games are added to a long list of releases on a daily basis, leaving the market fairly crowded. However, as the genre matures, more and more sub-genres are emerging. Inspired by the success of Peglin, our studio decided to take a swing at putting together a demo for a 'physics rougelike', combining classic mechanics of the genre with the arcady physics of a claw machine. We named the 'Dungeon Clawler' and it has managed to earn 100k+ wishlists in its first 3 months on Steam. This talk goes into detail on how the game was designed and marketed.

PHILOMENA: My talk is called "100'000 wishlists in 3 months - Weird roguelikes are taking over the
world." My name is Philomena. Thank you very much for the kind introduction. I am the co-founder
of stray fawn theater which is a 13 people based team in Zurich. We are in the same office as the
last speaker. We have made quite a few games in the last few years. We founded the studio back in
2016. The first game is niche a genetics survival game. Then we have Nimbatus. And our latest game
the wandering village which is a citybuilder simulation game with roguelike mechanics. My
whole team really likes roguelike mechanics. I gave a talk about this one last year. We have
been working on the game, same as star dust, since 2020. We are such a big team. In Switzerland I can
tell you it has been quite a financial burden to make this game. All of our studio's money we
made with the previous game went into this one. It coming out into 1.0 soon. Probably like beginning
of next year. And yeah, we are at this point a little bit relieved that after four years of
development we can soon move on to something else. Even though it has been a lot of fun making the
game. Our whole team every year is voting on what they want to do in the next two years as a studio.
During the whole development of this game we have been eyeing the whole roguelike deckbuilder genre
and we think it could be fun. We think we could make it in a smaller group like 2-3. We also felt
there is a lot. At this point there is a lot of roguelike tech -- deck builders. We looked around
if there were exceptions in the genre and when we saw Peglin we were like this is really it. Peglin
I think winze was one of the first roguelike deck builders that took the physical spin. Peglin is
almost like a different sub-genre of roguelike where we are starting to diversify within the
genre and opening up little sub-genres. We were like OK, so physic-based deckbuilders and what
are other game mechanics people know and are easy to understand that we could use in a deckbuilder.
We brainstormed with the team and one evening we came up with a why not claw machine. Somebody of
us said and then we would call it Dungeon Crawler and we were all like that's pretty funny. And then
we decided, yeah, we are actually going to make this game, and we are going to call it that. My
co-founder just he by himself went ahead and made this prototype. We have do what you want
afternoons every Monday and Friday afternoons where people are just prototyping. He went ahead
and made the prototype. We were like yeah, it is pretty fun. But it is also fun to start new
things so we quickly moved on, explored some other projects, and this was in the freezer
for a while. Then we took a team vacation to Japan last year. We went, all of us together,
for two weeks. We had the grandest time. Then we spent way, way, too much time in the arcades. Here
on the right side is actually my co-founder who had been making this little prototype. Then one
of our artists also got super addicted and we all took home like bags of prizes. We said it
is research. So we did it on company had to pay for our research in the arcades. We had a grand
old time. We found that OK, actually, these kinds of claw machines are super popular in Japan and
apparently also in China. I don't know exactly how it is in America but in Europe you only see
them maybe at like a local festival sometimes. Or sometimes in the restaurant. Then you can play
and they are super rigged and not fun to play at all. The ones in Japan were quite different
and the arcade was full of them. There were like five floors full of claw machines. The idea of
the genre that is pretty popular and the emergent Asian markets on Steam. China is the country with
the most users on Steam. We thought maybe there is something there and we should get this game
out of the freezer and keep working on it. The two of them who were super addicted to claw machines
teamed up and within three months took our little prototype we had previously made and turned into
this current state. From the beginning, it was very clear we wanted the arch to be pretty basic
so we could quickly and easily iterate and add new content to the game. Also because while they were
working on it full time, the artist was only there one day a week. He she has to be able to produce
the missing artwork fairly quickly. We decided we would launch the demo at the Steam deckbuilders
fest which was this March. 3-4 months work of demo, got it ready, setup the Steam page,
and did out reach to YouTuber's and Twitch streamers we had. Mostly people who played
previous games and some selected before would be a really good fit. Since then the game has
been snowballing. For us it is crazy because it is such a small team and such a small size compared
to the 13 people team for four years that we were used to. We didn't think we could pull something
like this off with such a small team. I wanted to share data with you because I thought it might be
interesting. I have really seen that this is our fourth game and all have been so different
in terms of how they appeal to players and how the wishlists are coming in. At the top is the player
number and we set the demo live at the same time we launched the Steam page. You didn't have to
think about triggering wishlist for demo releases back then. This has changed so maybe this wouldn't
have happened like this if we were to launch it now. We put the demo live and you can see
how the players evolved. You can see the wishlist is corresponding quite well to the demo players.
These were essentially the beats we had the game. When we revealed it was in the deckbuilder fest,
and we did international PR but also especially in Japan. It was picked up quite a bit by Japanese
press because I think they really liked the story of a bunch of western devs coming to Japan really
liking their arcades and then taking home their ideas and turning them into a game. That's why I
think we had like 10 times more PR coverage from Japan than from global in total. Also, this kind
of game is hard to sell the -- to the press. If it is six success, yeah, but not before. What
has been keeping the ball rolling for the game is just influencers. There is a very dedicated
influencer base like YouTube streamers for roguelikes that are really on the look out for new
and weird things which here again is why I think weird roguelikes are here to take over the world.
There is people really looking out for these types of games and picking them up even though we didn't
put a lot of effort and did no paid influencer campaign. They have really just been keeping
the game alive. And then Steam Next Fest came around and we did the big influencer push and
contacted quite a few thousand people to check out the game. And thanks to that, the game ended
up being the 11th most played game in the summer next fest which is insane to me. We were also in a
few showcases before the next fest which helped as well. On social media, the game hasn't really had
any success. We tried all kinds of channels. We had one Reddit post which went well but on social
it really doesn't work. For this game it has been all influencers and we are trying to participate
in Steam events as much as we can. The game has now reached 175,000 wishlists on Steam which is
beyond me. In the original press release we said if we could reach 10,000 we would buy a
claw machine for the office so I guess now we have to buy one. It is the 165th most wishlisted game
on Steam. The game, hopefully, looks like it, is coming out next month. We also decided because we
had a lot of feedback that people want to play it on mobile to port it to mobile right away.
This is the first time ever we have a mobile and PC same ship. PC will be early access. I am really
curious to see how it would hold up on mobile. I did quite a few calls with the devs of Peglin
and luck be a landlord and other roguelikes on how they are doing their monetization and most of them
recommended we should just go premium to start out with. So I am really curious if it will live up to
the sales on Steam in any way or if it will just be a tiny percentage. I am really, really looking
forward to the launch. I think we have quite a bit of time for questions if we have them.

PHILOMENA: Usually I am all for tell everybody your ideas. But with this one, I feel like I
have been stabbed in the back a bit. Ever since the summer next fest there is three mobile clones
out already which for me is a new level of crazy. I guess I am used to making more complex games. So
we did have the problem of people, for example, with wandering village, stealing our footage

they just took our whole itemization, all of our character designs, and like all of the balancing
and the games are free to play. That feels not so good when you are about to release your premium
game, right? In terms of when somebody makes inspiration and makes a similar game. Also for
example when the other claw machine roguelike was like announced, I looked at it and was like it is
completely different and just also a claw machine and I am fine with that. Maybe we could bundle
even with them down the road. I am fine with that. Just don't steal people's actual game content.
ALEXEI: I think bottling is a nice idea if you have that positive relationship
and share it. I think as a fan, if you hit on a funky genre like that and you enjoy it,
you often want to play other games riffing on the same idea. We have some questions. One
quick one is so does your studio do all your own PR? Or did you do any hiring to talk to press?
